analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal protection for workers who report unsafe conditions or refuse dangerous work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee after being referred there in June 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Occupational Safety and Health Act to make it illegal for employers to fire or punish workers for reporting injuries, illnesses, or unsafe conditions to OSHA, or for refusing work they reasonably believed could cause serious injury. It would have extended the deadline for filing a retaliation complaint from 30 days to 180 days, allowed complaints to be filed on a worker's behalf, and given the Labor Department power to order reinstatement, back pay, compensatory and exemplary damages, and payment of the worker's legal costs. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at hazardous jobs who report injuries or unsafe conditions and face retaliation would gain a longer window to file complaints, a faster path to relief, and remedies including reinstatement, back pay, compensatory and exemplary damages, and legal fees. Co-workers benefit when retaliation against safety reporting stops, because hazards get reported instead of hidden.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal for employers to discharge or discriminate against an employee for reporting any injury, illness, or unsafe condition to OSHA, adding that to the list of protected employee actions under the OSH Act.

Prohibits punishing an employee for refusing to perform duties when the employee has a reasonable apprehension that the work would cause serious injury or serious health impairment, a protection that did not clearly exist in the statute before.
Extends the deadline to file a retaliation complaint from 30 to 180 days, and lets other people file complaints on a worker's behalf, which matters for workers who fear filing themselves.

Requires a preliminary order providing relief whenever the Labor Secretary finds reasonable cause to believe a violation occurred, and authorizes orders to correct the violation, reinstate the worker with back pay, and award compensatory damages, exemplary damages, and attorney's fees.
Creates deadlines for the Secretary to investigate within 90 days and issue final orders within 120 days of a hearing, so retaliation cases do not drag on indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those whose workplaces have hazards, would bear the cost of stronger anti-retaliation rules: reinstated workers' back pay, damages awards, legal fees, and the cost of correcting violations found during retaliation investigations.

drawbacks.text: Exemplary damages and mandatory preliminary relief orders raise the stakes for employers even in contested cases, and the bill lets a reinstatement remedy in a preliminary order take effect before a hearing, which employers would argue punishes them before due process concludes.

The bill creates a fast-track administrative process with tight statutory deadlines for the Labor Department, and it is unclear whether the agency had the resources to investigate every complaint within 90 days, which could push cases into the hearing backlog instead.
The bill adds enforcement obligations and paperwork for the Department of Labor without any indication in the bill of new funding to handle the expanded caseload.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real but targeted: it protects workers who speak up about safety, a group the existing 30-day filing window and weaker remedies left vulnerable to being fired and priced out of a claim. The costs fall on employers and would show up as damages and fee awards in retaliation cases and as new demands on the Labor Department's caseload. A fair objection is that preliminary reinstatement orders take effect before a hearing, and that exemplary damages raise stakes beyond simply making workers whole.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Major Owens introduced the bill on May 18, 1999, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Representatives Clay, George Miller of California, Martinez, Payne, Kucinich, and Woolsey.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced.
On June 4, 1999, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no further action was taken.

The only remaining action in the record is the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 8, 1999; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: because the bill never advanced, the existing rules stood, with their shorter 30-day complaint window, no explicit protection for refusing dangerous work, and no provision for exemplary damages or attorney's fees. Workers who face retaliation for reporting hazards are left with the weaker, pre-existing protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who keep the weaker rules

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in June 1999.

for.name: Reps. Clay, Miller, Martinez, Payne, Kucinich, and Woolsey

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 18, 1999 and referred it to a subcommittee; the record shows no hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill during the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from June 4, 1999 onward; no further action was ever taken on it.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and no votes were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, mining services)
industries.note: These employers would face reinstatement, back pay, damages, and fee awards when they retaliate against workers who report hazards, and would lose the ability to remove a hazard by firing the person who reported it. Their interest in weaker anti-retaliation rules runs directly against workers' safety.

The bill allows the Secretary to order violators to pay complainants' attorney's fees and expert witness costs, expanding paid work for lawyers representing retaliation claimants. That fee-shifting is also the mechanism that makes the protection affordable for individual workers.

The bill expands the agency's role as the mandatory channel for retaliation complaints and gives it order-making and fee-assessment powers. Workers' protection would run entirely through this agency's investigation and hearing process.
